p01.argument: Line 8 does name the father's labor: 'my father nailed the boards down in thirty-one.' A reader could take the stanza as a tribute to his workmanship. But nothing in the poem says the speaker wants the buyers to value it, and the key's reading (something kept clean and out of sight under the rugs) sets up 'walls so thick no neighbor ever heard'.

Read literally, 'I was raised better than that' sounds like pride in a biblical upbringing, which supports [3]. The poem's irony undercuts that reading: being 'raised' in that house meant learning to cover things up. The key is better.
p01.stem_issue: This item overlaps heavily with Q11. Both test the same irony in the final line, so a student who sees it once gets both points.

p01.argument: The furnace sits in 'rusted robes', which could suggest neglect. But 'will not die' points to the furnace lasting, not to a coming breakdown, so [3] gets the furnace backwards.
p01.key_flaw: 'Outlast the people living there' goes slightly beyond the text. 'Will not die' shows the furnace is durable, but the poem never says it outlives anyone. The claim is defensible but stretched.

p01.argument: [1] says the neighbors knew and ignored the trouble. The text says the opposite: 'no neighbor ever heard'. They could not have known, so this option fails. The key's irony reading is supported by 'Everyone said so'.
Line 18, 'I was eleven', might tempt a careless reader to choose [1]. But 'was' is past tense, and the speaker drives off in a car (line 25), so she is an adult.

[2] has some basis: stanzas 3–4 do place the hearing and holding on the house ('what you heard'). But the speaker withdraws that charge in line 20 ('don't think I've come here to accuse you'), and nothing in the poem condemns the neighbors.
p01.stem_issue: This item overlaps with Q14. Both reward the same 'from house to complicity' reading.

p01.argument: Stanza 4 is literally framed as 'what you heard', meaning what the house heard. So there is a textual hook for [3]'s claim that the stanza takes the house's point of view. But the speaker is the one telling it, and the child was there too (she turned up the radio), so the key holds.
p01.stem_issue: Calling it 'the speaker's first-person account of the events in the fourth stanza' sits a little awkwardly with the stanza's own framing, which presents the events as what the house heard. The stem also points to line 13 when the account runs through line 15.

p01.argument: [2] might appeal because the house did hide the secret. But a jar has no will, so 'deliberate protector that chose' contradicts the vehicle of the simile. The device is correctly called a simile ('as a jar holds water').
[1] might seem plausible because the radio comes in the next line. But 'going small' describes 'my mother's voice', not the music, and the radio is being turned up, not fading.
[0] might appeal because the line sounds like a sincere disclaimer. But 'nothing wrong ever happened inside' contradicts stanza 4.
Someone could argue that the Lot's wife allusion is a new religious note. But the 'bishop' simile in line 3 already brings in a religious register, so the earlier stanzas do prepare for it.
p01.stem_issue: This item overlaps with Q2, which tests the same idea.

p01.argument: Nothing in the text supports the father controlling the radio. Line 17 explicitly gives that act to the speaker: 'I was the one who turned the radio up.'
p01.stem_issue: The phrasing 'the radio (line 15) and (line 17)' is ungrammatical.

p01.argument: [2] has some surface plausibility: the troubled family is gone, so the house might now be peaceful. But 'They'll mean it as a compliment' signals dramatic irony, which supports the key.
'Everyone said so' gestures at the town, but the poem never generalizes to other houses. [3] overreaches.

p02.argument: The second-person address to the father might suggest he is there in spirit. But 'your flask and your map' and 'tonight I'll tell you' show he is absent and the walk is a report to him.
'rubbed bright by someone's thumb' does suggest that visitors touch the post. But 'or weather' undercuts this rather than confirming it.
p02.key_flaw: 'Habit' is an overreach. The poem has only one instance of this self-correction, so 'tendency' or 'impulse' would be safer. It does not ruin the key.

p02.argument: Line 6 does move to history and landscape ('cinder laid across the fields'), and on the surface it reads as a plain fact. A reader who does not know that keys fasten rails might not see the implication about the keys and could pick this option.
p02.key_flaw: The key's reading depends on knowing that track keys exist only with the rails. That is technical railway knowledge the poem does not explain.
p02.stem_issue: Line 6 does not come 'directly after' line 3. Lines 4–5 and a stanza break come in between, so 'directly' is inaccurate. The item also needs outside knowledge of what track keys are.

p02.argument: No option competes. The stanza plainly states the plan to lie ('I'll tell you the keys are holding') and compares the lie to a track key.
'Of all the sleepers you are the last one / still on the line' has an elegiac tone. But 'tonight I'll tell you' shows he is alive.
p02.key_flaw: 'Care home' is an inference from the name 'Fairholme' plus 'brakes on'. It is reasonable but not stated.
p02.stem_issue: Line 28 is cited as evidence of track work, which depends on knowing what 'ganger' means (a foreman of a track gang). That is outside knowledge, though line 23 ('You pulled the last keys yourself') supports the point anyway.

p02.argument: The errand looks at first like a sign of confusion, since there are no keys left. But 'you knew' (line 23) reverses that reading, so the option is half right at best.
A reader might take the errand as a sign of dementia. But line 23, 'you knew', rules this out directly.
p02.key_flaw: 'Neither needs to name aloud' is slightly more than the text shows. We are not told that the father expects the lie, only that he 'taught' this kind of lie.

p02.argument: The wren is small, and the comparison is set against the 'cold' stone. But the spanner simile stresses a sudden, harsh noise, not delicacy.
p02.key_flaw: 'Even the wildlife recalls past labor' gives the memory to the bird. In fact it is the speaker's comparison that calls up the labor.
p02.stem_issue: The simile runs across lines 20–21 ('A wren goes off / like a dropped spanner'). Citing only line 21 is a minor imprecision.

p02.argument: Shoulder-high cow parsley and a routine nod from a dog walker clearly mark the line as overgrown and ordinary. None of the other options has any support.
Option 1 contradicts 'not the map' directly, and no other option is supported.
When she first reaches the empty cutting, the speaker could think his knowledge is out of date. But line 23 at once overturns that, and the stem asks about the primary function.
'Sleepers' and 'last one' carry a hint of death. But 'still on the line' and the later 'tonight I'll tell you' show he is alive.
p02.key_flaw: 'Dozing' is inferred. The text gives 'sleepers' and the television, not a direct statement that he is asleep. It is acceptable as wordplay.

p02.argument: A track key really is a wooden wedge 'driven / hard into the gap', so 'wedge' fits the literal image. But the poem's wedge holds things steady ('keep the heavy thing / from shifting'), while this option says it forces people apart.
p02.stem_issue: The metaphor runs over lines 30–33 ('the kind / a railway's made of...'), not only lines 31 and 33.

p02.argument: 'up to my shoulder' (her body in the field) set against 'brakes on' (his immobility) does contrast their bodies. But it shows neither her coming to an insight nor the point that his memory is intact, both of which the claim needs.

p03.argument: Line 21 says he asks 'every noon, the same / two words', and that repetition could suggest a habit he keeps up mechanically after hope is gone. But 'thanked him for the answer' points to deliberate courtesy, not something he does without noticing. The later finding that he 'slid sideways down the slats' toward the west road shows his hope was still active.
p03.stem_issue: The habit runs across lines 21-22 ('asked the postman, every noon, the same / two words'). Citing only line 22 is slightly narrow.

p03.argument: Someone reading 'lied' on its own might take it as suspicion of the grandfather's honesty. But line 19 describes the grandfather the boy wished he had ('a grandfather who... lied about the war'). It is not an accusation. The key fits the 'I wanted' construction.

The council does put the shelter on the bench's exact spot ('The new bus will halt where your boots halted'), which could be read as a memorial. But 'to make room for' and the bench being trucked 'to the depot' show displacement, not honor.
p03.key_flaw: The justification says the vigil was 'partly hidden'. That fits the afternoon waiting, but the key option itself only says 'open-ended'. This is a small mismatch but does no real harm.

p03.argument: 'I wrote at Easter' could be read on its own as dutiful letter-writing. But 'then I meant to write' plainly undercuts any pride. The key is solid.
p03.stem_issue: The clause starts in line 25 ('and I wrote at Easter'). Line 26 alone shows only the later stages, though the syntactic pattern is still visible.

p03.argument: In the afternoon the sun is in the west, so moving to the west end could be read literally as following the warmth. But the poem ties the west arm to 'the city road' and ends the stanza with 'to me', which shuts out a purely physical reading.

'Stopped clock' could suggest a life that stopped in forty-two. But the simile sits inside 'I was ashamed of you... I wanted a grandfather who...', so it is the boy's judgment. The key correctly gives it to the fourteen-year-old.
There is nothing to support this option. 'I let you think' is an admission of guilt, not reassurance.
p03.key_flaw: 'Late arrival' is slightly loose. The speaker never arrived while the grandfather was alive, and 'confession' is the stronger point. Still acceptable.

p03.argument: No other option links the evidence to the claim. Options 0-2 misread the details or overreach ('entirely forgotten Pavel').
p03.key_flaw: The key depends on the arm facing west, but 'that faces west, down the city road' is in line 32, not line 31.
p03.stem_issue: The cited line 31 ('the other arm, rubbed pale as soap, the arm') does not mention the west direction, which is the detail the key and its justification rely on. The citation should be lines 30-32.

p03.argument: In the Odyssey, Argos's master does come home, so a reader might connect the allusion to the 'triumphant homecoming' option. But nothing in the poem suggests Pavel returns, and the stanza stresses the women 'lowered their voices'. The key's humble, enduring loyalty is right.
p03.key_flaw: The justification says 'neither Pavel nor the grandson ever comes back to him'. The grandson does come back and sits on the bench ('Now I sit where you sat'), only after the grandfather's death. 'Comes back in time' would be accurate. Also, Argos's loyalty in Homer is rewarded with recognition, so the poignancy comes from the contrast with Homer, which the key could make clearer.
p03.stem_issue: The line glosses the allusion fairly well ('who lived to know his master's step'), but reading it fully assumes some knowledge of the Odyssey.

p04.argument: Clipped sentences could suggest strain or grief, but 'I had my reasons' plainly asserts choice, and 'I would not have had him looking back' confirms it was deliberate.
p04.key_flaw: The key adds a second claim about the last stanza that isn't needed, but that claim is accurate ('let his run downstream').

p04.argument: 'after tea' and the coal-boats could suggest time passing, but the poem never marks the move into night, and the contrast is about the tune.
'It is wrong' could read as a verdict on his ability, but lines 18-19 ('and that one holds') rule this out.
p04.stem_issue: The sentences in line 17 run on into line 18 ('He tries / another'), so the 'short declarative sentences' sit inside a longer movement. This is minor.

p04.argument: 'lifts its brown shoulder' gives the water a body, but nothing in the text suggests mourning. The image is one of waiting.
The speaker never contradicts herself. 'it was never for the want of notes' explains the gap rather than contradicting it.
The drying-yard is where she sang the ending, but she never teaches it to the boy: 'I keep it shut... I do not sing.'
He may be aware that she is watching, but the poem gives no sign he is performing for her. 'pleased with himself' points to his own satisfaction.
p04.stem_issue: Line 3 alone is cited, but the description continues into the simile in lines 4-5. This is minor.

p04.argument: She does recall singing with Tom, but 'I have it still' directly denies that she has forgotten.
'drag' often connotes reluctant effort. Still, the drivers take the tune up eagerly within days ('They will call it his by Sunday'), which undercuts reluctance.
p04.key_flaw: Towpath drivers lead the horses that haul the boats; they don't haul the boats themselves. The key's wording is slightly loose.

p04.argument: 'bending down' and the halt could suggest his skill failing, but 'as far as you' and 'He stops there too' tie the halt to Tom's own stopping point.
'drying-yard' points to a working setting, but it belongs to the remembered past and gives no time of day.
A boy standing on a lock-beam above deep water could suggest danger, but nothing in the text signals menace. 'waiting' and 'holds one foot' convey suspense.
She is Tom's widow, but she addresses 'Tom' and refers to the boy as 'he'. She is not speaking to her son.

p05.argument: Teodor gets a whole stanza of grief: 'He has died since. / I know it the way we know a frost,' and the poem closes with 'Forgive me, Teodor.' That could support a reading centered on mourning. But the claim that the note and envelope are 'the only traces' of his life goes beyond the text, and mourning is not the poem's main movement. The key fits the arc from the doubted 'kindness' to 'a prayer / that should not be answered.'

Half of the note, 'Do not let them dry out,' is literally about dryness, so [0] has a surface hook. But nothing in the poem ranks dryness above the cold, and the stem asks how the note relates to the final stanza. 'Good in poor ground' links to 'the long drought' and 'the world above gone wrong,' which supports the key.

The girl 'ate six of our red cousins' and was punished with a stay below, so a reader might carry the idea of punishment over to the seed. But the seed eats nothing and commits no forbidden act. 'At least they let her up for spring' sets the two cases against each other, which is what the key says.
p05.stem_issue: Recognizing the Persephone/pomegranate allusion takes some outside knowledge. Still, the poem gives enough ('underworld,' 'half of every year,' 'up for spring') to answer without naming her, so this is acceptable.

p05.argument: 'They tell me' does distance the speaker from its keepers. But nothing in the line or the poem reaches 'bitter fury.' The tone is wry and later becomes longing and guilt, so the key's 'wry doubt' fits.

No option is defensible. 'I want it so badly I almost crack' shows unresolved strain, not peace. Nothing physical happens to the vault. The line does not go back to cold imagery. The double meaning of 'crack' (germinating, and coming apart under strain) is well supported by 'made for one thing, which is splitting.'

'Twice a year the light comes on,' the 'coat as thick as a mattress,' the roll call 'where nobody answers,' and 'the dark shuts behind her' all point to the key. The schoolroom detail is a simile, not a sign that the place was once a school, and Dagny 'goes out humming,' not frightened.

Teodor clearly belongs to the past ('He has died since'), and Dagny is the present caretaker. But nothing ties her to the future, and the seed does not choose to look ahead rather than back. The contrast between impersonal routine and intimate care, carried by 'licked the flap' and 'salt and pipe smoke,' fits the key.
The bean names itself ('I am a speckled bean'), is still in storage ('for nine years'), and speaks to Teodor at the end. None of the distractors survives the text.

The mountain 'holds us,' which suggests guardianship. But it 'has never wanted / anything,' so it cannot share the seed's hope. The key correctly sets the mountain's lack of desire against the seed's longing.
p05.stem_issue: The personification runs across lines 22-24, not just line 22. This is minor.

p05.argument: 'Forgive me, Teodor' does show guilt, which gives [3] a foothold. But the guilt is for wishing disaster on the world, not for causing his death: the apology comes right after 'a prayer / that should not be answered.' The key's 'intimate loyalty' is backed by 'I can still taste him.'
p05.key_flaw: The phrase 'ruin he would never want' is an inference, though a fair one: he talked to rows and wrote careful instructions.

p05.argument: The poem is full of feeling and is not objective. It does not report current events in detail. It never enters Dagny's thoughts. The key is the only reasonable reading.
The stanza does mention disasters, but it ends in craving ('I want it so badly I almost crack'), not calm acceptance. The key's movement from purpose to cost to self-judgment matches the text.
p05.stem_issue: The stem stops at line 30, but the self-judgment the key refers to ('that should not be answered') falls on line 31. The range should be 25-31.

p05.argument: The coin simile ('to be worth something, never spent') clearly separates having value from being used. The distractors about wasted money, exhaustion, or wanting to be sold have no basis in the text.

A careful reader could argue that the nested guarding (envelope, box, mountain) suggests how valuable the seed is. But the tone is doubtful, not proud ('They tell me... a kindness'), and 'which is nothing, which is a breath' plays the duration down. The key's 'burial' reading, which points ahead to the underworld allusion, is stronger.
p05.key_flaw: The explanation lists 'foil' among the enclosures, but the foil envelope is in line 4, not line 5. The enjambment claim is correct: line 5 runs into 'for nine years.'
p05.stem_issue: The stem points to the enclosures 'in (line 5),' but the first enclosure (the foil envelope) is in line 4. This is a minor citation mismatch.

p06.argument: The ticket 'Harle and back, third class' might suggest she is saving toward a trip, which would make the marks a countdown. But the ticket's 'date gone by' and the fact that the count is 'not for the ones who leave' rule out a calendar of waiting.
One could read 'does not ask' as distance. But 'She means it kindly' and the water she brings up point to warmth, not a businesslike relationship. Nothing in the poem mentions rent.
'Now I am thorough' could sound like self-satisfaction. But 'Not one of them has taken me' rules out any escape, so 'proud' does not fit.
'some parlor I will never sit in' does hint at class difference. But the poem shows no envy of the owners. The point is the destination she is shut out from, which the key captures.
The distractors are contradicted by the text: the brother's window is 'empty', nothing in the poem mentions railway work, and the memory is not a light one.

The device is correctly called a simile ('like a drawer pulled open in the dark / and shut again'). No distractor has textual support. 'Offered' slightly overreads the image, but it is a reasonable reading.
p06.key_flaw: The key's reading 'offered' is a slight interpretive stretch; the image mainly suggests something brief that opens and then closes.

p06.argument: 'Mrs. Pruett thinks I mean to go' suggests, by contrast, that the speaker does not mean to go. That supports the claim only indirectly.
p06.key_flaw: The keyed quotation stops at 'to be sure' and leaves out 'that I am here,' the words that actually carry the evidence. The justification depends on line 31, which the option does not quote.
p06.stem_issue: The keyed quotation is cut off before the clause that matters most. Quoting lines 30–31 together would make the key cleaner.

p06.argument: Nothing in the poem mentions neighbors, open anger, or engines needing repair. The key is sound.
The distractors contradict the poem: she has not resolved to leave, and she is still keeping the tally. The key is right that 'to be sure' runs over into the next line.
No distractor is supported. Accounting is clearly the metaphor's field.
p06.key_flaw: 'A debt she owes' overreads the line. 'Keep the books' means record-keeping, a ledger; the idea of an unpaid debt is an inference beyond the text, though it is a plausible one.

p06.argument: A first-person speaker cannot reveal the landlady's private thoughts. 'thinks I mean to go' is the speaker's own guess. The option fails.
'wear that window thin' mentions wear. But it is Mrs. Pruett's figurative joke about the speaker's watching, not a physical detail of the room.
The ticket to Harle might suggest a traveler. But 411 tallies and a ticket whose 'date gone by' point to a long stay, not a brief one.
p06.key_flaw: 'Records departing trains' is slightly loose: she counts every passing train, including freight and night trains. Still, it is acceptable.

s01.argument: The detail about the shoes being 'resoled once in January' could, at a stretch, read as a ferryman sizing up whether a passenger can pay. But nothing in the text supports suspicion of fare-dodging: she 'paid again' every time.
'because it was money' could suggest he needs the income. But nothing in the text mentions financial trouble, and the bare circular reason fits the key's reading that he is avoiding curiosity.

The precise figures ('Seven hundred yards of greased wire', 'Eleven minutes each way') show a pride in mechanism. Still, the passage never says he admires machines, and the needle metaphor and the ending clearly point to a fixed, confined course.
s01.key_flaw: The key's phrase 'comes to mirror the narrator's own confined life' is an interpretation, but the needle passage and the ending support it.

s01.argument: 'By the fourth crossing the light on the water had gone the color of weak tea' marks time passing. No storm, pollution or nostalgia appears anywhere in the text.

'it did not trouble me' is a denial that gives itself away, much like line 62 in Q8. But it is still a claim of indifference rather than evidence of attention. The thermos detail shows a behavior he changed and then explained away, so it is stronger.
'A man could do worse' could be read as quiet pride in his trade. But 'could do worse' is modest, and option 3's 'superior to every other trade' overstates it.

'I wanted to see if it got easier, going over and over... It doesn't. It only gets the same.' This directly supports the key. The other options rely on things the text never says (the husband coming back by bus, the fare being too costly).
s01.key_flaw: 'Dull her trouble' supplies a 'trouble' the text only implies through the Detroit postcard; reasonable, but it is inferred.

s01.argument: Read literally, 'There was no call to' suggests calm acceptance. But the extra justification, which echoes 'it did not trouble me,' points to a denial that reveals the feeling.
We get only what he observes, her few lines of speech and Lucille's gossip passed on secondhand. Her name appears in line 10, so option 3 is false, and option 2 is plainly wrong.
He moved the thermos 'to the bench' while she was riding and now puts it back 'where it belongs,' which clearly restores the old order. Lucille runs a ticket booth, not a ferry.
'I have run her since the spring of 1931' and the past-tense telling support the key. October to March is a little more than 'one winter,' but close enough.
Stitching suggests joining the two banks. But the text says the hem 'never gets finished,' which rules out 'finished.' The metaphor is correctly named: 'the Corley is a needle.'
Working the count out 'on the back of a tide table' shows a man who keeps records. But the placement before her question mainly sets up dramatic irony around 'I didn't say.'
Her leaving could be read as unsettling his incuriosity. But the final clause, 'took them where they were going,' returns to his old indifference, and he says he 'did not watch the Cutbank side.'
s01.key_flaw: 'Travels without a destination' stretches a little: the ferry does have fixed landings. The key works only in the figurative sense, which the needle metaphor and the 'hem that never gets finished' support.

s02.argument: Until the reveal, Harrowby looks like a man of rules. He reads the offer 'as if the words were tolls', calls it 'only arithmetic' and blots and files the paper. A reader who stops before the kitchen scene could pick 'cares more for the Trust's rules.' But the stem says 'over the passage as a whole', and the Friday purchases ('The master's orders... so that Venn may have the pleasure of refusing it') rule this out.
s02.stem_issue: The watch-winding detail starts in line 13 ('He was a narrow, exact man') and runs through 15. The citation is slightly off but harmless.

s02.argument: The narrator does keep a 'private book' and writes in it 'that evening', so a diary-keeping clerk has some surface support. But 'I was then seventeen' and 'There are figures, I have since learned' clearly place the telling long after the events.

No other option holds up. The boats 'lay on their sides... like cattle that had given up', the coble is a 'long black scab' and the net has 'no fish in it to keep.' Nothing here suggests prosperity, a storm or the narrator's longing.

Turning a coin could suggest haggling over value, and Venn answers 'I've a catch most days.' That might read as bargaining. But he then turns the offer down outright ('The Trust may keep its shillings') and never asks for more, so this option fails.

The housekeeper writes the sum 'not in the household book but on a slip, which she pinned behind the clock.' The drawer is also full of unsigned papers. A literal reader might take this as hidden or falsified accounts. But the hidden figure is Harrowby's private kindness, not the Trust's records, and 'kept only by being left out' points to the key.

No other option holds up. The narration never enters Venn's mind; we only watch him 'through the window.' It does not give every character's motives equally, and the narrator is far from detached ('I thought him then the coldest man in Skelwick').

The kitchen scene takes place 'in the autumn', after the spring interview, so where it sits is simply chronological. The narrative is told in order throughout, so 'give the seasons a strictly chronological shape' is literally accurate as a description. As a statement of purpose, though, it misses the effect of the reveal.
s02.key_flaw: 'Reverse... Venn's refusal' slightly overreads. The refusal itself is not reversed; it is recast as something Harrowby expects and arranges for. 'Reframe' would be more exact.
s02.stem_issue: 'Withholds' suggests the story departs from time order, but the scene comes last because it happens last. Option 3 is also shorter than the others and not parallel with them.

s02.argument: Venn's fish do reach Harrowby's kitchen every Friday ('They were Venn's; I knew the tarred twine'). But nothing shows that Venn knows who is buying them or that he is grateful. The boy delivers them, and the arrangement depends on Venn not knowing.
'Like cattle that had given up' is correctly called a simile, and it suggests spent resignation. None of the other options fits.

Read literally, the phrase records that the narrator was a skilled penman, which suits a clerk. But it sits right after 'I thought him then the coldest man' and is set against 'I am afraid with some heat.' In that context it reads as self-irony.

Scales suggest fair measurement, so a reader might link the scale with the Trust's exactness. But the price paid is 'four times what they would fetch on the quay', which ignores the weighing, so the scale's meaning is turned upside down rather than standing for rigid fairness.
s02.stem_issue: Calling the scale a 'symbol' is somewhat generous, though it can be defended.

s02.argument: Of the four quotations, only the unsigned stack of earlier offers points to an offer that is repeated and refused. The others show Harrowby's manner or Venn's unease.

One could argue the housekeeper is only reporting what she has been told. But she quotes her master directly ('He says the Trust's offer is made each spring...'), so nothing suggests she misunderstands him.

s03.argument: 'He made sure of that' does show that Aurelio deliberately kept Portuguese from her, so someone could stretch this into a claim that the letter was written to shut her out. But she also says 'He wants it read to me while he can still hear it,' so the letter is clearly meant to reach her. Option 0 contradicts the scene.

The original appears in italics-style free indirect form at lines 36-38, and the substitute is spoken at line 44. A reader might briefly think the letter had two versions. But Aurelio's 'That is not what I wrote' rules out any revision by him.
s03.stem_issue: The written sentence actually runs from line 36 to line 38 ('and I would go again'). The stem cites lines 36-37, which is a minor line-reference slip.

s03.argument: She is standing 'by the radiator with her coat still zipped,' and both details could literally point to cold. On that reading option 3 is the surface meaning. Still, the text never says the room is badly heated, and the later moment when she sits on the bed supports reluctance rather than temperature.
s03.key_flaw: 'Ready to leave at any moment' slightly overreads a zipped coat, though the core idea of not settling in is sound.

s03.argument: Placing a miscarriage beside a drunk-driving plea might hint at the strain of such work. But 'I have held to it' states fidelity outright, not doubt. Nothing points to grief or contempt either.
s03.key_flaw: 'The canon has held whatever she had to say' is awkward. She renders other people's messages, not her own. The idea is fine but the wording is muddy.

s03.argument: 'The only Portuguese interpreter in Halsey County who will drive in snow' could suggest she was the last resort on a bad day. But 'the agency called me' marks her as a hired professional, not a volunteer.
s03.stem_issue: The opening sentence starts at line 1, not line 2.

s03.argument: The canon's wording is repeated, which a careless reader might take as speech. But it is plainly her thought ('the card said'), and Dana does not respond to it.
'Eu sei' does admit what she did, so it could be read as a quiet apology. But it is not 'open,' and an admission is not an apology. The key's 'private acknowledgment' is more accurate.
The words 'frozen,' 'gray chop,' and 'plates left overnight in a sink' all support stillness and neglect. None of the other options has textual support.
s03.stem_issue: The simile continues into line 7, so the cited lines 5-6 are slightly too narrow.

s03.argument: 'A small complaint' could suggest a faulty machine. But 'as if it, too, had been asked to work past its hours' ties the image to tiredness, not malfunction or neglect.
s03.stem_issue: The personification runs from line 23 to line 25, not just line 24.

s03.argument: Option 1 is only plot summary, and options 2 and 3 are absolute claims or claims the text does not support. The key is specific and well supported.
The hesitation does resolve, but into an altered reading, not a faithful one. The text contradicts option 0.

The concentrator and the plow are ordinary sounds of the place, so 'relief' is a surface reading. But 'scraping it bare, scraping it bare,' placed right before the substitution, shows the images working as foreshadowing, not as a break in tension.
She touches his knee and laughs, which a reader could inflate into full forgiveness. But 'wholly' and 'every injury' overstate it, and the image of ice she doesn't trust argues against it.
s03.key_flaw: Saying the change was 'produced' by the altered letter is somewhat too causal. Dana already 'unfolded her arms' at line 39, because of the narrator's pause and before the false line is read. She also softens at the suit request on the third page.

s03.argument: 'The way you sit on ice you don't trust' strongly supports the reading of a fragile thaw. The other options are literal or have no support in the text.

s04.argument: Option 3 picks up the stopped-time imagery and the narrator's dispute with the ledger ('I had looked back; I am quite certain of it'), which questions whether memory can be trusted. But 'every human memory' and 'no event... can ever be known' go well beyond the text. The key covers the ledger, the guarded voice ('never sentimental about clocks') and the practical-sounding ending.

'A dealer does not pay more for clean glass' does show she knows something about the trade, so option 1 has a surface case. But one remark does not show 'thorough, expert' knowledge, and it misses why she says it: she gives a money reason to avoid touching his things. The key is the best answer.

No distractor has support. The text never compares Pell's skill to the father's, and nothing suggests Pell is dishonest; his reasoning ('none of them running... brings it down') is fair. The narrator never winds the clocks ('I have not wound any of them'), which rules out option 1. The key fits the ending: 'his watch went with him, and the shop was quiet again.'

'As a man holds his breath outside a sickroom' does bring illness to mind, and the father was ill at the end, so option 2 has a slight link. But the simile describes someone waiting outside the sickroom, not the sick man's own fear, so 'vigil' (the key) is the better reading. The key's 'the shop' slightly widens the image beyond the long-case clock, but the 'row of deacons' simile backs that up.
s04.key_flaw: The key attributes the vigil to 'the shop', while the simile describes only the long-case clock. This is a minor stretch, supported by the 'deacons' simile.
s04.stem_issue: The stem is garbled: 'The description of the long-case clock that (lines 12-13)' leaves out the quoted words (e.g., 'held its pendulum still, as a man holds his breath outside a sickroom'). As written, the sentence does not parse.

s04.argument: The flashback does come before Pell's arrival, so option 3 states something literally true. But nothing in the text builds suspense about his offer. The key is backed by 'when he looked at all' and 'It was always a clock that was nearly going', both of which the ledger later overturns.

'Hush, Nell... though I had said nothing' could, at a stretch, be read as a fond running joke, which is option 3. But the text gives no sign that she enjoyed it; 'when he looked at all' and 'It was always a clock' sound like grievance. The key fits: he speaks to her unprompted, and she reads it as dismissal.
s04.stem_issue: The stem is garbled: 'The father's habit of saying (lines 21-22)' leaves out the quoted words ('Hush, Nell... She's nearly going').

s04.argument: The distractors misdescribe first-person narration. The narrator is guarded and arguably unreliable, so she is not neutral (option 0). She has no access to her father's thoughts (option 1), and the point of view never shifts (option 2). The key is correct.

Pell had just raised his price to forty-five, and 'Not at present' could look like haggling, which is option 1. But she sends him away ('You'll forgive me the trouble') and pockets the cash book, which shows the change is emotional. The key is right.
s04.stem_issue: The stem is garbled: 'that she is (lines 50-51)' leaves out the quotation ('not ready to sell').

s05.argument: A reader who stops at the boy's early suspicion ('I had decided the account was a joke') and at her calm admission that she lets the watch stop might call her manipulative. But the 'Paid' entries with Pruitt's initials show that he chose the arrangement knowingly, and nothing suggests she is exploiting him.
s05.key_flaw: 'Swindle' slightly overstates the boy's view. He thinks the account is 'a joke he played on himself', not fraud. The key is still clearly best.

s05.argument: The narration is fairly restrained, so a reader might call it detached. But it shows the boy's inner state ('I did not intend to say ma'am in any soft way'), so it is not cool or neutral.
s05.stem_issue: The stem says the point of view is limited to what the boy noticed at the time, but the narrator is a retrospective adult ('I keep a shop of my own now'). This does not change the answer.

s05.argument: The house is cold, which could suggest poverty, so the stopped clocks might look like neglect. But she says she simply forgets to wind them, and the dead pendulum and flag point to grief, not lack of money.
The cold house might suggest he just lost his nerve or his words. But he says 'I had my sentence ready,' so he did not forget it.
s05.key_flaw: 'Without explanation' is a little off. The narrator gives a false explanation ('because she had cried'), and the photo and flag imply the real one. The key still works if it means no stated reason.

s05.argument: Choice 3 overstates it. 'For the rest of his life' is contradicted by 'I still tell people I would have asked her.'
'I keep a shop of my own now' rules out telling the story the same night.
A reader might read it as shame, but 'though she had not cried' denies that she cried at all, so he could not have made her cry. The line shows self-deception.
In the myth, Penelope has suitors, which might suggest a courtship role for Pruitt. The text gives no support for this.
s05.key_flaw: The allusion works partly by contrast ('Mrs. Danner was not weaving anything'), and Penelope's husband did come home. The justification's phrase 'she undoes the watch' is loose, since she only lets it run down. The key's reading still holds.

s05.argument: A leaning house could suggest it is falling down, but the clause 'as if it were trying to hear' makes the personification about listening, not decay.
'Paid' with Pruitt's initials overturns the joke theory and does not confirm it.
A flag could suggest military pride, but 'stiffness of a thing nobody touches' points to avoided grief, and nothing mentions a long tradition.
The adult narrator does show Pruitt's mercy openly in his story. But 'I still tell people I would have asked her' contradicts 'fully converted' and 'speaks openly.'
'Looked into it for a long time' might suggest searching for a flaw, but 'already knew was sound' rules that out.
The other choices contradict the text (Pruitt's clumsiness, his greed) or overgeneralize ('all old men').
s05.key_flaw: 'A debt of care' is a slightly interpretive way to describe Pruitt's view, but it is reasonable.

l01.argument: Mentioning August rates 'with breakfast' could be read as pride in the hotel's high season, as though she is correcting a traveler who thinks her rooms are cheap. But the lines end on 'It's May. I'm full,' which shuts the bargaining down. Nothing in them defends the hotel's standing.
l01.key_flaw: Saying she answers 'each raised offer' stretches it a little, since lines 30-31 answer only the seven-dollar offer. The pattern holds across the scene as a whole, though.

l01.argument: Vera's flat 'Pumps.' (line 55) comes before Walt's correction and signals that she doubts him. It is a plausible competing 'confirmation.' The option is ruined by 'proves that he has never sold a pump at all,' which line 56 ('I was in pumps') contradicts.
l01.key_flaw: Line 56 shows the claim was out of date and partly a cover, not invented outright. 'Not fully reliable' fits that, so the key holds.

l01.argument: Opening the drawer and closing it again could be read as a signal to the stranger that she is close to giving in. But no price has been named yet, and the gesture does not point to any 'exact price.' The hesitation reading in the key fits better.
Naming the daughter could look like a revelation, but Walt already says 'I only want to see her walk in.' He knows the bride is his daughter. The option has nothing in the text to support it.

Putting the key on the bills does stress money, but the ending undercuts a profit-only motive: she puts the money in the apron pocket with the hem pins, not in the till. 'Only motive all night' is plainly false.
l01.key_flaw: 'Sparing her the touch' reads a little more feeling into it than the text states, but it is a reasonable inference.
l01.stem_issue: The direction actually runs across lines 66-67, not just line 67. Minor citation slip.

l01.argument: Nothing suggests the audience knew who he was earlier. The heading stays STRANGER until Vera says 'Walt.' No option competes with the key.
l01.stem_issue: The heading change only affects readers of the script. In performance the audience learns his name from Vera's spoken 'Walt.' The key's wording ('in the script') handles this acceptably.

l01.argument: Her instant, precise recognition could suggest she had imagined this meeting before. But nothing points to rehearsal, and 'spent eighteen years waiting' goes beyond the text.
l01.key_flaw: 'Reluctant' is an inference. She calls his habit 'decent,' which is warm as much as reluctant. Still a defensible reading.

l01.argument: Turning the photograph face down when he enters, and again after looking at it, could be read as a steady refusal to share family life with him. 'Steady refusal to let Walt learn anything at all' fails, though, because she tells him freely about the daughter's room, dress and wedding.
l01.key_flaw: The text never has her show Walt the photograph. At line 54 she 'looks at it' herself and puts it face down again. 'Let him glimpse it' is an overreading. The 'shield' half is supported, and the 'divided impulse' is better grounded in her looking at it herself and in what she tells him in speech.

l01.argument: Nothing supports leaving before the ceremony. Missing the bus would keep him in town longer. No real alternative.

You could argue she stays guarded: she still sends him up the back stairs, and 'The house is asleep' sounds like a reminder about the sleeping guests. But it echoes his own habit, which she described in lines 51-53, so it is not 'exactly as guarded.' 'Only' her guests also ignores that echo.
l01.stem_issue: The final instruction starts on line 73 ('Mind the door') and ends on line 74. Minor citation issue.

l02.argument: 'God forgive me' could be read as a conventional pious formula for the sin of pride in general. But the context is that the pupils' success is credited to a master who is dead, and 'I had been so careful' points to guilt about the deception, not a general belief that all pride is sinful.

Ann 'did not once look at me' and the class's 'Nobody laughed. Nobody breathed' could suggest the children were coached. But nothing in the text mentions any drilling, while their silent, shared reaction fits tacit protection of her.

No option competes. 'Nobody laughed' rules out comic relief, and the text gives no sign of resentment or of Hetty knowing less than the others. The question reveals the secret ('shall Miss hear our spelling'), and Dask 'write[s] a single line in his book'.

Option 3 claims Dask noticed nothing. His irony ('under its present master', 'I trust Mr. Penhallow's chest will hold') and his line about the coat show he understood. Option 1 is a plot summary, not a thesis, and option 2 overgeneralizes.
No option competes. 'six years of letters... all answered in a hand that had once been my brother's and was now mine' fits the key directly.
l02.key_flaw: 'Written in her dead brother's hand' slightly overreads the line. 'A hand that had once been my brother's and was now mine' could mean she copied his handwriting, or more loosely that she took over his role as the person who answered letters.
l02.stem_issue: Lines 15-16 by themselves do not show that the brother is dead. The reader needs the introduction and lines 6-9/44 for that, so the cited line range is narrower than the evidence the key relies on.

l02.argument: No option competes. The Regulations require 'a certificated master' and say a woman 'might assist but not keep it', while the pupils' strong showing proves she can do the job. Nothing in the text mentions wanting to leave, a curate demanding confession, or a dislike of teaching.

'The moth will have it' could be read as a warning of loss. But the claim being supported is about permission, and 'It wants wearing' urges use rather than threatening anything. Option 2 is too literal, and option 3 depends on outside generalizations about novels.

'They have not yet learned what is wanted' could hint that he expects the children to give away the truth. But 'trick' and 'betraying' don't fit his kind, grave conduct at the end. The key, preferring unrehearsed testimony, is the best reading.

No option competes. Line 23 says the chair was one 'which I had never sat in', and the ending reads 'I put it on... sat in his chair, and heard the spelling'. She is teaching, not mourning or acting out of fear.
